doc.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024

title: Dave Brubeck's 1976 South African tour and its conditions
summary: The New Brubeck Quartet toured on conditions of a black support act, a black bassist (Vic Ntoni) and unsegregated audiences; Cathy acted as liaison.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Had Dave played in South Africa?

Yeah. In 1976. And it was just before the cultural boycott had been announced and there was some opposition to it but by — well mainly what this did is we went on tour in South Africa as The New Brubeck Quartet. That was Dave, Chris on bass and trombone, and Dan, and our agent at the time Associated Booking Corporation (ABC) — I never go into this kind of detail with journalists but I suppose for an archival interview it’s good to know that kind of stuff — and parenthetically every imaginable pertinent document on anything we talk about can be found in the Brubeck Collection at the Wilton Library, Wilton, Connecticut. Anyway so our agent had signed a contract that we hadn’t seen because he had that signing power, and Dave said we wouldn’t go. And the agent said, “Well then that’s going to be litigation and you don’t want that.” But what Dave said, “Well I’m not going anyway unless we establish certain conditions. And these were that we would have a local black supporting act and that because Chris played trombone we absolutely needed a black bass player. Well we absolutely needed a bass player but it was understood what we really needed was for a local South African black person to be on the stage simultaneously with us as well as a support act, or the opening act as they say in the States, support act in kind of the rest of the Anglo-sphere, and that the audiences could not be racially segregated. Now in the back of Dave’s mind was they can’t meet these conditions and we won’t go. But they did. Except in one city, ironically, and that was Durban, which is where I ended up, at what was then the University of Natal. But we did the tour and became very good friends with Vic Ntoni — spelled N-T-O-N-I — who was the bass player and he had worked with Abdullah Ibrahim, known as Dollar Brand at the time. When Victor came to the States, came to the U.S., with help from Dave and the family to study at Berklee, he hooked up with Hugh Masekela who was living in the Bronx at the time. And I should say that well a lot of this is in the book. I’ll try not to repeat too much of it, but also my future (at that time) future wife Catherine Shallis or

Cathy Morphet — Shallis was her maiden name. Cathy Morphet from her second husband — first husband. I’m further down the line — M-O-R-P-H-E-T — went on the road as kind of a liaison person but the thing is with the local contacts that she had and on the surface the local contacts were some music people that she knew. She had always been involved with jazz, and kind of less overtly with a kind of liberation organization people who were, you know that was all kind of off-the-record stuff but constantly taking the temperature — were we going to suddenly hit a boycott situation or were we going to get shut down by the regime. We were kind of in an uncomfortable place, because — vulnerable to attack from the government or from the left. So Cathy’s contacts were valuable in explaining our position, explaining the contract I just explained to you.
